title: Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto (Finland) - TSV/238/2022
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A taxpayer (the data subject) requested access to all personal data related to their taxation for the tax years 2017–2022 from the Finnish Tax Administration (the controller) on 9 May 2022. In addition, the data subject requested all internal processing and log data and notes, as well as information on who processed the data at any given time and why. In a second access request sent on the same day, the data subject also requested a copy of their personal data processed by the controller.
The data subject repeated their access request on 2 June 2022 and additionally requested that the controller investigate whether the data subject’s data had been accessed without justification or unnecessarily during the tax years 2017–2022. The controller responded to the data subject’s requests for access to personal data and log data on 2 June. It provided the data subject with an extract of their personal data, customer details, as well as information on income tax, property tax, inheritance and gift tax, and motor vehicle tax. The controller refused to provide the data subject any log data: the data subject had not demonstrated why they would be considered an party whose right, interest or obligation is concerned within the meaning of Section 11 of the Act on the Openness of Government Activities.
The data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA on 15 June 2022 and stated that they had reasonable grounds to suspect that the controller had not provided them all the information they requested within the time limit specified in Article 15 GDPR. The data subject claimed they had only received general descriptions of the controller’s processing practices instead of the requested personal data and log data.
In November 2022 and irrespective of the complaint to the DPA, the controller issued a decision refusing to provide the data subject the requested log data, as the data subject had not presented any grounds prescribed by law based on which they would be entitled to this information. The data subject has requested the log data again on 4 April 2023. The data subject appealed the controller’s decision to Helsinki Administrative Court, which overturned the decision and referred the case back to the controller for reconsideration on 28 November 2023. 
Following this decision, the controller provided the data subject information on when their personal data had been processed in May and July 2025. However, the controller refused to disclose the identity of the employees who had processed this data. 

Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA held that the controller had violated Article 15(1) GDPR as it had not fully complied with the data subject's request to be informed of the times and purposes of the processing of their personal data. In particular, the controller had failed to provide the data subject the log data from 1 January 2017 to 13 May 2019. However, the DPA did not order the controller to provide the data subject this information as all log data older than that of 14 May 2019 had already been deleted.
The DPA referred to the CJEU’s decision in case C-579/21 Pankki S and pointed out that the data subject has the right to be informed of the times and purposes of any queries made regarding their personal data under Article 15(1) GDPR in light of this judgment. As the decision had changed the DPA’s interpretation of Article 15(1) GDPR, the DPA considered that there were no grounds for reprimanding the controller for failing to provide the data subject this log data and only provided the controller guidance on the matter.
Second, the DPA concluded that the data subject did not have the right of access to information on the identity of the controller’s employees who had processed their personal data. According to the aforementioned CJEU decision, the disclosure of employees’ names to the data subject therefore requires that the disclosure of the data be essential for the data subject to exercise their rights. In the present case, the data subject had not invoked any such grounds.
Finally, the DPA held that the controller had complied with its obligations under Articles 12 and 15(1) GDPR regarding other information than data on the times and purposes of processing contained in log files. According to the DPA, the controller had provided the data subject the requested information on the processing of their personal data related to taxation as well as a copy of this data.

title: Datatilsynet (Denmark) - 2025-441-4624
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Jan Nygaard (the controller) reported a data breach to the DPA within which they clarified that the controllers systems could not be accessed and that their servers had been compromised. 
In order to investigate the DPA requested further details. The controller submitted reports prepared by the Computer Security and Incident Response Team (CSIRT) which addressed the breach. The CSIRT noted that the controller was subject to a ransomware attack, that the servers were isolated from the network after identifying the attack, and that the malicious actor had gained access via a terminal server. Furthermore, the report revealed that there were multiple attempts to gain access to user accounts. Eventually the actor successfully gained access allowing them to download data from the systems, encrypted files and left a ransomware note demanding payment. 
The controller underlined that in response to the breach report it had implement technical and organisational measures such as, shutting down the server, implementing multi-factor authentication and tightening password requirements. The affected data subjects were also notified of the breach and clarified that personal data such as email addresses, names and phone numbers were compromised. Following the first notification, more types of personal data were posted on the dark web, and included dates of birth, contact information, social security numbers, drivers license and passport information of customers and employees. Data subjects were subsequently informed about this.
During its investigation it was discovered that more than 48,000 data subjects were affected by the breach amongst which 194 were employees. The controller clarified that the information of approximately 25,00-30,000 individuals should have been deleted at the time of the breach, and that no one had been assigned responsibility to ensure compliance with such. Namely, because the data should have been stored in a specific IT system where no issues with deletion requirements existed.
The controller explained that storage on the server drive between 2009 and 2022 should have ceased and the server decommissioned, the data within should have then been deleted in 2018. Nonetheless, whilst employees were instructed not to store personal data on this server, due to habit they continued to do so. Furthermore, some data should have been deleted earlier but it was not possible for the controller to determine this with more specificity. The controller further explained that the storage of personal data on the server was justified by the need for archiving and compliance. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the controller did not adequately assign someone to be responsible ensuring compliance with the retention and deletion of information. Similarly, the DPA held that the controller lacked the implementation of necessary measures which could have addressed the failure to delete data or shortened the period during which deletion did not occur due to an error. The DPA held that this could have prevented by the controller, if they had implemented an appropriate storage limitation pursuant to Article 5(1)(e) GDPR and thus deleted the data.
The DPA acknowledged that the failure to delete the data no longer needed was partly due to employees not following instructions. Nonetheless, the DPA also emphasised that the controller could have detected non-compliance with such by implementing the right measures. 
Moreover, the DPA held that whilst the implementation of deletion rules by the controller demonstrated the intention to ensure timely deletion in accordance to Article 5(1)(e) GDPR this was not sufficient without the monitoring of the measures to verify that they are appropriate and effective for the intended purpose (Article 32(1)(d) GDPR).
In light of the foregoing, the DPA reprimanded the controller for failing to implement a procedure for the regular testing, assessing and evaluation of the effectiveness of implemented measures, and failed to remove the unnecessary drive which constituted a violation of Articles 5(1)(e) and 32(1) GDPR.

title: IMY (Sweden) - 2025-6466
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a multitude of complaints from individuals regarding Legal Newsdesk’s search service which provided and made accessible information concerning decisions from Swedish courts and government authorities. The website provided a search database of documents from criminal and civil cases, penalties, decisions not to prosecute amongst others, covering the period of 2008 onward. The database was updated with thousands of documents daily, and certain older documents were weeded out over time.
The controller implemented changes to the website to include concise articles and information based on public records, providing comprehensive court coverage and in-depth reporting of Swedish legal cases. Using the search function, users were able to enter a name or personal identification number and find associated cases and documentation. Paying users were also able to access hidden content such as case numbers and contact information for the relevant court found within the documents.
In its investigation the DPA also assessed the complaints it received. Throughout it was discovered that search results provided name, age and city of the person being searched for as well as terms relative to the content of the documents. Search results about criminal cases would also include information about the charge, the penalty, case number and contact information.
In its defence the controller submitted that it operates the website under a publication certificate and under the responsibility of the publisher. The purpose of the controller’s website was to inform the public about how courts rule in criminal cases. The controller clarified that its source material consisted primarily of criminal case rulings which were made public. Furthermore the controller emphasised that reporting on crime, punishment and the administration of justice was at the core of journalism, which comprised the core purpose of the business.
The controller did not provide the DPA with information regarding the total number of published documents which contain information falling within the scope of Article 10 GDPR. The controller deemed this information business critical.


Holding[edit | edit source]
Primarily, the DPA assessed whether the processing by the controller is carried out for journalistic purposes. Following the CJEU’s ruling ND v Legal Newsdesk, it was decided that an activity consisting of making public documents available to the public in exchange for payment can be considered processing of personal data for journalistic purposes in accordance with Article 85(2) GDPR only where it is intended to disseminate information, opinions or ideas to the public. This requires the material to undergo a certain degree of editing or processing before publication, and publication in accordance with press and professional ethics. Finally, the factual claims and circumstances must be verified prior to publication. 
Applying this to the controller, the CJEU ruled that the investigation in this case did not support the conclusion that the controller was processing for journalistic purposes. Furthermore, the DPA held that neither after the changes to the controller’s search service could the processing be considered to pursue a journalistic purpose. Especially because the service was seen to be the same type of service with the same purpose as before the changes, and thus did not fulfill the criteria established by the CJEU to constitute processing for journalistic purposes. 
The DPA held that the controller processes personal data related to criminal convictions in its search service which ultimately constitute criminal data within the meaning of Article 10 GDPR. For such processing to be lawful, the DPA emphasised that it must be authorised by national or EU law.
In accordance with national law, criminal data may be processed by parties other than public authorities where it is necessary to comply with archival regulations, where it is necessary to establish, assert or defend legal claims or to fulfill a legal obligation. Following this, the DPA found that the controller did not demonstrate an applicable legal basis as required by Article 10 GDPR to process criminal data, neither can a legal basis be established.
Finally, the DPA found the controller in violation of Article 10 GDPR regarding its the processing of criminal data in its search service without a legal basis and thus issued a reprimand.

title: Datatilsynet (Denmark) - 2025-41-0136
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA initiated an investigation on its own volition, into the processing of personal data of customers when they use the shopping app of Coop Denmark A/S (the controller). The DPA requested information from the controller regarding its processing practices, legal basis, purpose pursued, whether data is shared with third parties, and if yes what data.
In its submission, the controller clarified the purposes for which it processes personal data through the app amongst which membership administration was listed. The controller further clarified that for the purposes of membership administration it based its processing on performance of a contract pursuant to Article 6(1)(b) GDPR. The controller also explained how the app is used and how users may purchase through the use of the app, particularly in connection to the personal data processing undertaken.
The controller provided additional information regarding location data and the necessity to process such for the purposes of knowing which store an individual is in and be provided with the correct prices. It expressed that this allows for all stores to be able to manage inventory and attributes each purchase to a specific store, the location data is not stored. For members who do not wish to share the location via their device a QR was provided for which allowed the controller to know which store the member was in. 
Furthermore, the controller also listed Article 6(1)(f) GDPR as a legal basis for processing in order to prevent, investigate and prosecute fraud involving Scan & Pay. The controller undertook a balance of interests and deemed their interests legitimate and thus necessitating such processing.
Finally, the controller mentioned the processing of personal data through the use of cookies for marketing purposes which is based on consent. The controller clarified that no data is disclosed to third parties, and described the cookie mechanism to include two different checkboxes: accept all in a red box and accept selected in a light-colored box.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the collection of information and personal data of customers, for the purpose of administering membership and compiling statistics and carbon footprints was compliant with the requirements of consent of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR and for the performance of a contract under Article 6(1)(b) GDPR.
Moreover, the DPA found that the controller did not demonstrate the objective necessity required by Article 6(1)(b) GDPR, to process location data for the performance of the contract. The DPA reemphasised the option to scan a QR code offered by the controller, and stated that such processing should have instead been based on freely given consent.
Furthermore, the DPA held that the controller could not rely on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR for processing location data from members’ cell phones for marketing purposes. Once again the DPA held that the controller should rather rely on consent as processing of location data, regardless in what form, is intrusive for data subjects. In that regard, the DPA found that the controllers interest in marketing products were less compelling than the need to protect data subjects, and that the controller could have implemented less intrusive means.
Finally, the DPA held that the data collection through the use of cookies for marketing purposes undertaken by the controller did not comply with Article 6(1)(a) GDPR. Specifically, the DPA found that the choice of colour, namely red and white for the accept all button influenced and nudged users into providing consent. 
Therefore grounds to reprimand the controller for processing location data without an adequate legal basis, and for the use of cookies to collect user consent for marketing purposes which was deemed incompatible with Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

title: APD/GBA (Belgium) - 308/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Two police officers (the data subjects) where photographed while performing their duties outside of an airport’s departure hall. 
The controller is a natural person who regularly resides in Spain and, at the time the photograph was taken, was dropping off his family at the airport. 
The controller published the photograph, along with comments, in three closed Facebook groups connected with the airport’s traffic situation. In accompanying comments, the controller criticised the data subjects’ enforcement of the new traffic and parking regulations. He described them as unfriendly, arrogant and insufficiently understanding. 
The data subjects submitted a complaint to the Belgian DPA. They argued that they were identifiable, had not consented to the photograph or its publication, and had suffered harm from the accompanying comments. 
The controller argued that he had exercised his freedom of expression by informing the public about the changed traffic situation and criticising how the data subjects enforced it. He removed the Facebook posts after the DPA informed him about the complaint.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA considered whether the processing pursued journalistic purposes within the meaning of Article 85 GDPR and Article 24 of the Belgian Data Protection Act. The DPA explained that journalistic activities are not limited to professional media organizations but include all activities intended to communicate information to the public, regardless of the medium used.
The DPA judged that the controller sought to inform the public about the new parking situation and expressed his opinion about the data subjects’ conduct. The photograph showed the data subjects performing a public function in a public space, without depicting them in a compromised situation. The comments criticised their professional conduct without personally identifying or compromising them. Moreover, the dissemination was limited to three closed Facebook groups whose members had an interest in the airport traffic situation. Therefore, the DPA found that the processing pursued exclusively journalistic purposes.
Second, the DPA assessed the legal basis for processing of personal data for journalistic purposes. The controller did not rely on consent under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR but on legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. His interest consisted in exercising freedom of expression under Article 10 ECHR in the context of a journalistic activity.  
Regarding necessity, the DPA found the photograph and the accompanying comments suitable for communicating the controller’s views and their publication in three closed Facebook groups limited the audience.  
In balancing the competing rights of data subjects and controller, the DPA held that: 

The posts contributed to a debate of public interest concerning the new traffic regulations.
Policy officers acting in uniform and exercising public authority could be regarded as public figures who shall tolerate public scrutiny and criticism.
The photograph was taken in a publicly accessible place, from a distance and without unlawful means.
The officers were shown neutrally while performing their duties and were not identified by name.
The comments did not exceed the degree of criticism that public officials could reasonably be expected to tolerate.
The controller removed the posts once he was informed of the complaint.
Consequently, the data subjects’ rights to the protection of their personal data did not outweigh the controller legitimate interest in exercising his freedom of speech.
Therefore, the DPA held that the controller did have a legal basis for sharing the photo and comments in the three closed Facebook groups and did not violate Article 5(1)(a) GDPR in conjunction with Article 6(1) GDPR.

title: Datatilsynet (Norway) - 24/01411-15
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The Norwegian DPA received a complaint by the data subject against Social Garden AS (the controller) concerning the publication of members’ photos and other profile information, among which name, age, and place of residence, on the homepage of the website skeiv.no, a dating site operated by controller. The objective of skeiv.no was for members to connect with thousands of other queer people and to meet ‘like-minded people’. 
Even though the complaint concerned only skeiv.no, the DPA included in its investigation also other websites operated by the controller that processed special categories of data, including kristendate.no/dk/se. The objective of Kristen.no/dk/se was to connect members with Christian values and traditions. 
On both websites, anyone could access the homepage without registering or logging in. Visitors could view photographs and profile information of new and active members, as well as their latest posts. 
The controller claimed that the legal basis was consent. During registration, data subjects were required to tick a box accepting the membership agreement and the processing of data. Registration could not be completed without ticking this box. However, the membership agreement, located at the bottom of the registration page, contained no information about the processing of personal data. Data subjects had to consult the privacy policy separately. 
The issue was whether the public publication of members’ profile information, including photos, on the homepage of skeiv.no and kristendate.no/dk/se constituted processing of special categories of personal data under Article 9 GDPR and whether valid consent has been obtained for this processing under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
Whether profiles on skeiv.no and kristendate.no/dk/se constituted special category of personal data
First, the DPA assessed whether information indicating that someone has a member profile on skeiv.no constituted information about that person’s sexual orientation. 
The DPA considered that the website was marketed primarily towards LGBTQ+ community Consequently, information indicating that a person was a member of the website allowed an inference that they likely belonged to this community. The DPA held that such indirect inference was sufficient to reveal information concerning a person’s sexual orientation. 
Second, the DPA assessed whether information indicating that someone has a member profile on kristendate.no/dk/se constituted information about that person’s religion.
The DPA noted that the website was marketed primarily towards people with Christian values and traditions and that its users were predominantly Christians. It therefore considered that information indicating membership of the website allowed an inference that that person was Christian, thereby indirectly revealing information concerning their religious beliefs. 
The DPA concluded that the public disclosure of members’ profiles on both websites constituted processing of special categories of personal data under Article 9(1) GDPR.
Whether the controller obtained valid consent 
The DPA assessed whether the controller had obtained valid consent for the publication of members’ profiles under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR. Since the processing involved special categories of personal data, the relevant exception was Article 9(2) GDPR. The DPA considered that if consent did not satisfy the requirements of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR, it could not constitute valid consent under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR.
Therefore, the DPA examined whether consent was freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous within the meaning of Article 4(11) GDPR. 
First, regarding freely given consent, the DPA noted that members were required to accept the membership agreement and the processing of personal data to register on these websites. The DPA emphasised that consent must involve genuine freedom of choice and shall not be made a condition for accessing a service where processing in unnecessary for its performance. 
The DPA considered that publicly displaying member’s profile was not necessary to participate in online dating services, which could operate without making members’ photographs and other profile information accessible to non-members. Moreover, the publication primarily served to promote the websites to potential new members rather than facilitating interactions between existing members. The DPA concluded that consent was not freely given and therefore invalid. 
The DPA held that the controller lacked a valid legal basis for processing under Article 6(1) GDPR and a valid exception under Article 9(2) GDPR for the public disclosure of members profiles. 
The DPA fined the controller 140,000 NOK (€13,258.96).

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - Expert Petroleum S.R.L.
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Expert Petroleum S.R.L. (the controller) suffered a cyberattack on its IT infrastructure. This incident led to the unauthorized access and disclosure of sensitive personal information, such as health and financial data, belonging to a significant number of individuals (the data subjects). The controller then submitted a data breach notification to the DPA, prompting the authority to initiate the investigation.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA held that the controller violated Article 32 (1)(b)GDPR, Article 32 (1)(d) GDPR, and Article 32(2) GDPR. The DPA found that the controller failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure the ongoing confidentiality and security of its processing systems.
Second, the DPA considered that the controller did not regularly test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of its security measures. The DPA noted that this lack of appropriate security protocols allowed a cyberattack to successfully compromise the IT infrastructure, resulting in the unauthorized access to and disclosure of the data subjects' sensitive personal information.
Furthermore, the DPA exercised its powers under Article 58 (2)(d) GDPR to impose specific corrective measures. The DPA ordered the controller to implement access monitoring and logging systems for its IT infrastructure, requiring a minimum 30-day retention period for activity logs. Additionally, the DPA mandated the exclusive use of a Virtual Private Network (VPN) and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for any external access to the network.
In October 2026, the Romanian DPA decided to fine the controller €8,000 (RON 42,788) for the breaches of Article 32 GDPR.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - ASAM S.A
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
ASAM S.A. (the controller) implemented a modernized video surveillance system that systematically monitored its employees (the data subjects). The events unfolded beginning with the controller installing numerous cameras throughout the workplace—including in highly private areas such as locker rooms, restroom entrances, and dining spaces—without conducting a prior Data Protection Impact Assessment or adequately informing the data subjects. Furthermore, the controller retained these recordings for excessive periods.
Subsequently, a specific data subject submitted a formal access request to the controller, seeking access to their personal data, which explicitly included video footage related to their professional activities. When the controller failed to provide a complete, written response or supply the requested information, the data subject filed a formal complaint with the DPA. This complaint directly prompted the authority to launch an investigation, which ultimately uncovered both the mishandled access request and the controller's broader unlawful surveillance and data retention practices.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA held that the controller violated Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Article 12(1) GDPR, Article 12(2) GDPR, and Article 12(4) GDPR. The DPA found that the controller failed to provide a complete written response to the data subject's access request and did not supply the requested personal data, which included video footage. The DPA further argued that the controller lacked adequate internal measures to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights regarding video surveillance processing.
Second, the DPA considered that the controller breached Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, Article 5(1)(e) GDPR, and Article 5(2) GDPR, alongside Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, Article 12 GDPR, and Article 13 GDPR. The DPA emphasized that the controller unlawfully monitored employees by installing cameras in areas where privacy must be guaranteed, such as locker rooms, restroom entrances, dining areas, and offices. The DPA also determined that the controller retained the video recordings for an excessive period exceeding 30 days without justification and failed to provide proper transparency and information to the data subjects.
Third, the DPA established that the controller violated Article 35 GDPR. The DPA noted that the controller deployed a modernized, large-scale video surveillance system equipped with smart functions to systematically monitor employees, but failed to conduct the mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) prior to commencing the processing.
Furthermore, the DPA imposed several corrective measures. The DPA ordered the controller to fully fulfill the data subject's access request, implement a formal internal procedure for handling GDPR requests without delay, dismantle cameras located in private spaces, restrict video data retention to a maximum of 30 days, inform all data subjects completely, and finalize the required DPIA.
In October 2026, the Romanian DPA decided to fine the controller €1,000 (RON 5,337) for the breaches of Article 15 GDPR and Article 12 GDPR, and €4,000 (RON 21,348) for the breaches of Article 5 GDPR, Article 6 GDPR, Article 12 GDPR, and Article 13 GDPR. The DPA also issued a formal warning for the breach of Article 35 GDPR.

title: UODO (Poland) - ZSZZS.421.9.2019
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
In April 2019, the Polish DPA inspected a non-public primary school (controller) attended by children aged 7 to 15. The controller filmed pupils around the clock with cameras in its hallways, two classrooms and the gym. The cameras were installed between 2013 and 2015, after parents complained about how teachers treated pupils. The controller said the cameras protected pupils and property and that it did not have enough staff to supervise pupils at all times.
An external IT specialist maintained the CCTV system and made copies of recordings. However, his data processing agreement did not cover CCTV. The controller’s record of data processing activities and its risk assessment did not cover CCTV either.
During the proceedings, the controller relied on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and Article 6(1)(d) GDPR, pointing to its duty to ensure safety under the Polish Education Law Act (Prawo oświatowe). It also argued that it did not need a record of processing activities under Article 30(5) GDPR, because it had about 50 staff. In 2025, it fixed the processor agreement, the record and the risk assessment, but it kept the cameras running.


Holding[edit | edit source]
Lawfulness of processing
The DPA held that the controller had violated Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6(1) GDPR, because it had no legal basis for filming these pupils.
First, Article 6(1)(c) GDPR did not apply. A legal obligation must follow clearly from a provision of law, as required by Article 6(3) GDPR. The DPA agreed with the controller that Article 108a of the Education Law Act only applies to public schools. The other provisions the controller relied on created a general duty to ensure safety, but they did not oblige anyone to process personal data, let alone to use CCTV. The controller had also not shown that CCTV was necessary. Referring to EDPB Guidelines 3/2019 on video surveillance, the DPA held that the controller could have used less intrusive measures, such as hiring staff to supervise pupils. Thus, a lack of staff did not justify CCTV.
Second, Articles 6(1)(d) GDPR did not apply. According to Recital 46, vital interests can only be relied on when no other legal basis is possible, for example in humanitarian emergencies. The situation at the school was nothing like that.
Third, the controller had expressly denied relying on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and had not carried out a balancing test. Under Recital 69, the burden of proof lies with the controller. Finally, the DPA held that informal parental support and a parents’ vote did not amount to consent under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR. The processing was also not necessary to perform an education contract under Article 6(1)(b) GDPR. Furthermore, a private school’s commercial activity was not a public task under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR.
Processor agreement
The DPA held that the controller had violated Article 28(3) GDPR. The IT specialist could see the live footage and made copies of recordings. This meant he processed personal data on behalf of the controller, thus being a processor. The DPA rejected the controller’s claim that it never handed over recordings. The 2018 agreement did not cover the CCTV processing, and the violation lasted until the controller extended the agreement in 2025.
Record of processing activities
The DPA held that the controller had violated Article 30(1)(b) GDPR because the CCTV processing and its purpose were not in the record. The exemption in Article 30(5) GDPR did not apply. The cameras recorded and stored footage around the clock, so the processing was not occasional, even if the recordings were only rarely viewed. Moreover, the exemptions only applies where there is no risk at all, not merely no high risk. The controller itself called the risk “negligible”, which meant it accepted that some risk existed. Referring to Recital 38 and Recital 75, the DPA stressed that processing children’s data always creates a risk.
Security of processing
The DPA held that the controller had violated Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR because, until 2025, its risk assessment did not cover the CCTV system. This left out risks such as the involvement of the processor, the availability of the recordings and the disposal of hard drives.
Corrective measures
For the violations of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6(1) GDPR, the DPA treated the processing as a single set of related operations under Article 83(3) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 52,511 (€12,500). Additionally, the DPA also also ordered the controller to stop filming pupils in classrooms and in the gym.
For the violations of Article 28(3) GDPR, Article 30(1)(b) GDPR and Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR, the DPA only issued warnings under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR. The controller had already fixed these problems during the proceedings, and the data subjects had not suffered any harm.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 815
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Since 2023, Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (the controller) offered a feature called “Get camera roll suggestions when browsing Facebook”, which suggested photos and videos from data subjects’ camera roll as potential posts while browsing Facebook. 
Following a complaint by the Centro Consumatori Utenti of Bolzano in July 2025, the DPA launched an investigation. 
The infringement related to Article 122 (1)(2) of the Italian Data Protection Code (implementing Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive) in conjunction with Articles 6,7,12,13 GDPR for having accessed information stored on data subjects’ mobile devices, specifically photos, videos and related metadata, without consent or any other legal basis, and without having informed data subjects in a manner that ensured their effective awareness.
The controller contested the application of Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code as it would have required the use of electronic communications network and the transmission of information from the device. The controller argued that this feature operated solely on-device, reading only metadata and without transmitting any data to the controller’s servers, and that the processing was limited to the suggestions made by the user.
Moreover, the controller argued that: 

Access to the gallery required authorisation at operating system level, which data subjects’ granted either in full or limited it to selected content. Operating system authorisation constituted an affirmative action on the part of the data subjects and free, specific, informed and unambiguous consent, relating to a single purpose and revocable at any time.
The feature processed the most recent photos and “basic metadata” (date and time the photo was taken, photo marked as favourites, photo type and orientation).
When data subjects’ granted device authorisation, the option “Get suggestion from your gallery while browsing Facebook” was set to on, whilst for other data subjects it was off by default.
When the feature was active, the controller presented the user, while browsing Facebook, which basic sharing suggestions were drawn from their gallery.
It did not base the processing on consent but on contractual necessity for data subjects with full legal capacity and legitimate interest for minors.
The processing took place entirely on the device and did not involve the processing of special categories of data.
Transparency was ensured by the privacy notice and the information provided within the product.
Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA rejected the controller’s objection to its jurisdiction, clarifying that the GDPR one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply to violations of national provisions implementing ePrivacy Directive. 
As regards the legal basis invoked, the DPA held that access to information stored on terminal equipment cannot be justified on the grounds of legitimate interest or on the grounds of contractual necessity but only on prior consent of data subjects. 
Concerning the data subjects' consent to the feature, the DPA found that access to the camera roll was requested through a single permission, valid for the entire app and for multiple features with different purposes. The permission included a generic warning “enable other features” that did not let the data subjects’ know they were also agreeing to suggestions from photo gallery. Thus, the data subjects were not in a position to understand, before granting access, that they would be enabling the controller to systematically scan their photo library in order to suggest content to post.
Moreover, this feature was enabled by default. When granted, the permission allowed the app to access the entire photo gallery, on a permanent basis, without the data subjects’ or the DPA being able to verify which information was actually used. 
Likewise, the DPA also held that accessing information stored on data subjects’ devices required their free and informed consent, regardless of whether the information is subsequently transmitted or harm occurs, and that consent must be given for each distinct purpose and cannot result from silence, inactivity or pre-ticked boxes (Article 122 Italian Data Protection Code, implementing Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive). 
Therefore, the DPA fined the controller €805 million taking into account the approximately 20 million data subjects affected in Italy, the duration of the infringement, a previous decision against the controller in 2019, and its limited cooperation during the investigations. 
The DPA ordered the controller to obtain separate and specific consent for this feature, explain its purpose, the implications for accessing the camera roll and how to disable this feature. It also ordered the controller to comply within 60 days, report the initiatives taken within 30 days and the measured adopted within 90 days.
The DPA reserved the possibility of separately investigating a feature introduced in 2026 allowing camera roll content to be processed in the cloud.

title: OLG Hamburg - 7 U 70/22
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A real estate entrepreneur (the data subject) held the position of director and managing director at two companies between 2007 and 2013. The data subject had changed their last name after stepping down from these positions. The data subject’s father had taken over the roles of director and managing director, and the companies had subsequently made headlines due to allegations of delayed filing for insolvency and suspicion of fraud.
The data subject’s current name appeared under the pages concerning the aforementioned companies on a service that analyses European companies’ mandatory disclosures. The data subject requested the operator of this service (the controller) to remove their current name from the entries in September 2021, which the controller refused to do. The controller argued that it only processes personal data available in public registers and stated that displaying the data subject’s current name on its website served the public interest in transparency and security in commercial transactions.
The data subject filed a lawsuit against the controller before the Hamburg Regional Court (LG Hamburg), claiming they had a right to erasure under Articles 17(1)(c) and 21(1) GDPR as they had objected to use of their current name on the controller’s service and there were no overriding legitimate grounds for the processing. In addition, the data subject claimed rectification under Article 16 GDPR and injunctive relief.
The regional court dismissed the lawsuit. Following this, the data subject appealed the decision to the Higher Regional Court Hamburg and requested the deletion of their current name from the entries concerning the two companies.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The higher regional court granted the data subject’s claim and held that the controller should have deleted the data subject’s current name from its website at the latest during the court proceedings. According to the court, the data subject was entitled to the erasure of their personal data under Article 17(1)(c) GDPR in conjunction with Article 21(1) GDPR.
The court concluded that the data subject had already objected to the use of their current name in their written submissions for the present proceedings: the data subject had argued that it was potentially detrimental for them to be associated with companies facing publicly known criminal allegations. 
Furthermore, the controller had not demonstrated any legitimate grounds for the processing that would override the interests, rights and freedoms of the data subject. The court held that using the data subject’s current name on entries concerning companies that he had worked for under a different name constituted a significant interference with the data subject’s rights. In the court’s view, the public interest in transparency invoked by the controller did not extend to the data subject as they had worked for the companies a considerable time before the criminal allegations.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00034/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Pelayo Seguros (the controller) reached out to the DPA informing them of a detected data breach which resulted in the unauthorised access to their information system. The data breach consisted of a mass data query which resulted in access to customers personal data stored in the controllers systems, including name and surname, ID number, and contact details. The credentials of the user who was caused the attack and all traffic coming from that IP address were blocked in an attempt to resolve the breach. The data breach lasted two days and it was discovered that the data was not encrypted, anonymised or protected in a way which would not allow for the identification of the individuals. 
A data subject submitted a complaint to the DPA after they received notification of the data breach. The DPA initiated an investigation into the matter and requested additional information from the controller.
The controller clarified that the user to whom the credentials belonged was an exclusive agent representing an insurance agency, and that these were the credentials which were compromised and thus led to the breach. The controller further explained that the application affected by the breach was one through which claims for Motor and Miscellaneous insurance were registered. In order to access the applcation a user must either register a claim or resolve issues of access permission.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that this breach affected the confidentiality of personal data which manifested in the form of unauthorised access and exfiltration of the data. Whilst the controller detected the breach very quickly, it only became aware of the publication of the personal data after receiving a phone call that the data was published on the dark web.
The DPA held that the username and password access mechanism provided by the controller had limitations, especially where this data is combined with privileged access. Furthermore, the DPA emphasised that pursuant to the data breach, it was made aware that the data was not sufficiently encrypted, anonymised or protected to prevent unauthorised access.
Ultimately, the DPA found that the controller was unable to demonstrate that it has complied with its obligation to adopt appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure the data. In light of the foregoing the DPA held that the controller violated Article 5(1)(f) GDPR by failing to comply with the security standards required.
Initially, the DPA imposed an administrative fine of €40,000 on the controller. Pursuant to Law 39/2015, a Spanish law concerning administrative proceedings, the DPA informed the controller that it may acknowledge liability and make a voluntary payment of the proposed fine. This action reduces the imposed fine by 20% (€32,000). The fine can be reduced by a further 20% if the controller acknowledges liability and makes the payment in time. The controller opted for both and reduced the fine by 40%, paying the reduced sanction amount of €24,000.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - BT Direct IFN SA
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Metropolitan Life Asigurări Metlife Europe (the controller) utilized the services of BT Direct IFN SA (the processor) to handle insurance documentation belonging to a significant number of insured individuals (the data subjects). The events unfolded beginning with the processor mistakenly transmitting the data subjects' insurance documentation to unauthorized recipients instead of the rightful owners over a continuous period of three months. This operational error directly resulted in the unauthorized disclosure of and access to the data subjects' personal information, specifically their names, dates of birth, and insurance certificate numbers. Upon discovering this security incident, the controller submitted a formal data breach notification to the DPA to officially report the processor's transmission errors. Subsequently, this notification prompted the DPA to launch a thorough investigation directly into the processor to assess the adequacy of its technical and organizational security measures prior to issuing its final decision.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA held that the processor violated Article 32(1)(b) and Article 32. The DPA found that the processor failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk of its processing activities.Second, the DPA considered that this lack of appropriate safeguards directly resulted in the unauthorized disclosure of and access to the data subjects' personal data. The DPA emphasized that this continuous operational failure caused the misdirection of sensitive insurance documentation to unauthorized recipients over a prolonged period of three months.Furthermore, the DPA exercised its corrective powers under Article 58 (2)(d) to mandate operational changes. The DPA ordered the processor to actively monitor the data processing activities of the personnel acting under its authority, ensuring strict compliance with internal working procedures to prevent similar security incidents in the future.The Romanian DPA decided to fine the processor €3,000 (RON 15,833) for the breaches of Article 32 GDPR.

title: OLG München - 18 W 839/26 Pre e
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject (operator of a law firm) had a business profile on a business review platform (the controller), which contained several reviews about the law firm. Following three complaints from the data subject, the controller removed the challenged reviews. The data subject had argued that the reviewers were not former clients and had never used its services.
Following the removals, the controller added notices to the data subject’s business profile stating that two to five reviews had been removed following complaints about defamation under German law. The notices appeared in the reviews section of the profile and included a link to an explanatory page.
The data subject argued that the notices wrongly suggested that the removed reviews contained defamatory statements or excessive criticism. She also claimed that the notices could give users the impression that the law firm regularly challenged negative reviews without justification. The data subject therefore requested an interim injunction requiring the controller to remove the notices and refrain from publishing them again.
In May 2026, the regional court rejected the request for an interim injunction. The data subject appealed that decision.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The court dismissed the appeal and confirmed that the data subject had no right to require the controller to remove the notices or refrain from publishing them again.
First, the court considered whether Article 17 GDPR provided a basis for the requested injunction. It noted that the notices themselves constituted personal data within the meaning of Article 4(1) GDPR because they contained information relating to an identifiable natural person. Publishing the notices therefore constituted processing of personal data under Article 4(2) GDPR.
However, the court found that none of the grounds for erasure under Article 17(1) GDPR applied. In particular, the processing was not unlawful within the meaning of Article 17(1)(d) GDPR.
It also considered the notices accurate under Article 5(1)(d) GDPR. It explained that the controller's linked information page clarified that German law allowed businesses to challenge reviews where the reviewer could not establish a customer relationship. Consequently, the term "defamation" did not exclusively refer to excessive criticism or false statements made by actual customers, it also covered negative reviews published without an underlying business relationship. The notices therefore did not create a misleading impression.
Second, the court held that the processing was lawful under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. The controller and its users had legitimate interests in making the removal of reviews transparent. 
The court acknowledged that the notices affected the data subject's professional reputation, however, the notices appeared only in the reviews section, contained neutral wording and did not disclose the specific content of the complaints or the reviews. It therefore considered the impact on the data subject limited to its professional and public sphere and concluded that the data subject's interests did not override the legitimate interests of the controller and its users.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - TURISM LOTUS FELIX SA
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
TURISM LOTUS FELIX SA, a tourism company (the controller), suffered a ransomware attack on its IT infrastructure after threat actors exploited a remote connection lacking multi-factor authentication.
The attack resulted in unauthorized access to the personal data of a significant number of the controller's employees and clients (the data subjects). The compromised data included identification, contact, reservation and accommodation, SPA/wellness appointment and service, billing, financial-accounting, and contractual data, as well as email addresses, user accounts, access rights, and health data collected in connection with SPA/wellness services.
Following the incident, the controller submitted a personal data breach notification to the Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) pursuant to Article 33 GDPR, prompting the DPA to initiate an investigation.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) held that the controller violated Article 32(1) GDPR and Article 32(2) GDPR. The DPA found that the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk of processing. Specifically, the DPA established that leaving a remote connection unprotected by multi-factor authentication allowed threat actors to execute a ransomware attack on the controller's IT infrastructure, resulting in unauthorized access to the personal data—including health data—of a significant number of data subjects.   Second, the DPA evaluated the circumstances of the infringement against the criteria for imposing administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR. The DPA concluded that the severity of the case warranted imposing an administrative fine on the controller.In October 2026, the Romanian DPA decided to fine the controller €5,000 (RON 26,649) for breaching Article 32(1) GDPR and Article 32(2) GDPR.

title: APD/GBA (Belgium) - 314/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
On 6 October 2025, the data subject requested the removal of images of her that were used by a company (controller), to show as an example of how workwear should be worn. These images were displayed in the controllers’ offices and used in one of its instruction videos. This request for removal went unanswered. According to the controller, the data subject gave consent for being photographed. On 19 November 2025, the data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA.


Holding[edit | edit source]
On 10 November 2026, the DPA held that documents revealed the data subject did not give consent for the use of her image, and that she sent her request by letter to the controller. Therefore, the DPA ordered the controller to comply with the request of removal under Article 17 GDPR within 30 days, based on Article 58(2)(c) GDPR and Article 59(1)(5) WOG.
